items.followUp: Explain why atomic radius generally increases down a group.

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in nuclear charge while added electrons enter the same main shell.
rubric.description: Across a period, proton number increases and electrons are added to the same shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both the increasing nuclear charge and that electrons enter the same shell.

rubric.why: Links stronger attraction to the decrease in atomic size.
rubric.description: The stronger nuclear attraction pulls the electrons closer, so atomic size decreases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stronger attraction and resulting decrease in size.

modelAnswer: Across a period, the number of protons increases while the added electrons enter the same main shell.
The stronger nuclear attraction pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus, so atomic size decreases.

items.followUp: What is shielding effect, and which electrons shield the valence electrons?

rubric.why: Recognizes that effective nuclear charge is the net positive attraction experienced by an electron, particularly a valence electron.
rubric.description: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by an electron in an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as a net positive charge or attraction experienced by an electron.

rubric.why: Includes the effect of shielding by other electrons on the nuclear attraction.
rubric.description: It is the nuclear attraction remaining after the shielding effect of other electrons is considered.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the charge or attraction is reduced by shielding from other electrons.

modelAnswer: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by an electron in an atom.
It is the nuclear attraction remaining after the shielding effect of other electrons is taken into account.

items.followUp: Why are noble gases generally unreactive?

rubric.why: Identifies the complete outermost shell as the key feature of noble-gas configurations.
rubric.description: Noble gases have a complete outermost electron shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that their valence shell is complete, usually an octet or duplet.

rubric.why: Explains the stability or importance of the configuration for other atoms.
rubric.description: This configuration is stable; other atoms gain, lose or share electrons to attain it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the complete shell to stability or to the tendency of other atoms to attain a noble-gas configuration.

modelAnswer: Noble gases have a complete outermost electron shell, which makes their electronic configuration stable.
Other atoms gain, lose or share electrons to attain a stable noble-gas electronic configuration.

items.followUp: How do stronger intermolecular forces affect the energy needed to boil a liquid?

rubric.why: States the effect of stronger intermolecular attraction on boiling point.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces result in a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stronger forces raise the boiling point.

rubric.why: Explains the relationship by referring to the energy needed to separate molecules.
rubric.description: More energy is needed to overcome the attractions between molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that more energy is required to overcome the intermolecular forces.

modelAnswer: Stronger intermolecular forces result in a higher boiling point.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces and separate the molecules.

items.followUp: Which atom has the higher electronegativity, H or Cl?

rubric.why: Checks the stated electronegativity value for hydrogen.
rubric.description: Hydrogen has an electronegativity value of 2.1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the textbook value 2.1 (accept equivalent reported value 2.2).

rubric.why: Checks the stated electronegativity value for chlorine.
rubric.description: Chlorine has an electronegativity value of 3.0.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the textbook value 3.0 (accept equivalent reported value 3.16 or 3.2).

items.followUp: Define diffusion and give one example of it in gases.

rubric.why: Defines diffusion by the direction in which particles move.
rubric.description: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing movement from higher to lower concentration.

rubric.why: Distinguishes effusion as the escape of gas through a small opening.
rubric.description: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the passage or escape of gas through a tiny opening.

modelAnswer: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole.

items.followUp: At what condition does a liquid boil, and how does increasing vapour pressure affect its boiling point?

rubric.why: States the condition at which boiling occurs.
rubric.description: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that vapour pressure equals the external pressure at boiling.

rubric.why: States the inverse relationship between vapour pressure and boiling point.
rubric.description: At a given temperature, a liquid with higher vapour pressure has a lower boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the inverse relationship.

modelAnswer: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
At a given temperature, a liquid with higher vapour pressure has a lower boiling point.

items.followUp: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 0.5 mol of solute in 2 dm³ of solution.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of molarity as amount of solute per volume of solution.
rubric.description: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ (litre) of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition in terms of moles of solute and volume of solution.

rubric.why: Checks the formula and units for molarity.
rubric.description: Formula: M = n/V, where n is moles of solute and V is volume of solution in dm³; the unit is mol dm⁻³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula and an appropriate concentration unit.

modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ of solution.
Formula: M = n/V, where n is moles of solute and V is the volume of solution in dm³.
The unit of molarity is mol dm⁻³ (or mol L⁻¹).
